raw_case_text:
A five-year-old boy was admitted in Namazi Hospital, Shiraz, Iran with severe abdominal pain, jaundice and low grade fever. Similar symptoms were reported in his family about 30 days ago. He had abdominal pain and vomiting from 20 days before admission; his jaundice worsened and developed from 10 days ago. At the time of admission he was very sick with fever and yellowish discoloration of skin and sclera. He was very irritable due to abdominal pain. In the physical examination he had normal growth parameters and his vital signs were as follows: temperature: 38oC, pulse rate: 100/min, respiratory rate: 30/min and blood pressure: 100/60 mmHg. In the abdominal examination, a large mass was palpated in the right upper quadrant (RUQ) with severe tenderness. 
Initial laboratory investigations showed elevated liver enzymes: AST: 516 U/L, ALT: 722 U/L, alkaline phosphatase: 1930 U/L, total bilirubin: 5.3 mg/dL, direct bilirubin: 3.9 mg/dL, total protein: 7.7 g/dL, albumin: 3.8 g/dL, WBC: 8000/mm3, Hb: 11.9 g/dL, platelet: 426000/mm3, CPR: 6 mg/dL, ESR: 40 mm/h. Coagulation studies revealed PT: 13 sec, PTT: 34 sec and INR: 1. Serum amylase, blood sugar and serum sodium, potassium, BUN and creatinine were within normal range. Venous blood gas analysis revealed: pH: 7.5, HCO3: 30, and PCO2: 37.9. Blood and urine cultures were negative. Serology of viral hepatitis was positive for HAV IgM, and other viral markers were negative. Serology titers for typhoid and brucellosis were negative. Abdominal ultrasonography showed normal size and echogenicity of the liver, with significantly distended gallbladder (span 130 x 50 mm) with the fundus of gallbladder near iliac crest. The thickness of gallbladder wall was normal and no stone was detected. The hydrops of gallbladder was confirmed by ultrasonography (Figure 1).
Due to fever and toxic condition, he received antibiotic ceftizoxim and metronidazole. After the third day of admission, his fever and blood culture became negative and antibiotics were stopped. Surgical intervention was not required in the patient. After five days, general condition and abdominal pain of and jaundice improved and he was discharged with close follow up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 5-year-old boy presented in Shiraz, Iran, with a 20-day history of severe abdominal pain and vomiting, 10 days of worsening jaundice, and low-grade fever.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The child developed abdominal pain and vomiting 20 days prior to admission, followed 10 days later by progressive yellowish discoloration of the skin and sclerae and low-grade fever.
subjective.past_medical_history: Normal growth parameters. Family history was notable for similar symptoms of jaundice and febrile illness among family members approximately 30 days prior.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for severe abdominal pain, irritability, vomiting, jaundice, and low-grade fever.

objective.physical_examination: On admission, the child appeared very ill and irritable due to abdominal pain, with icteric skin and sclerae and normal growth parameters. Vital signs: temperature 38 °C, pulse rate 100/min, respiratory rate 30/min, and blood pressure 100/60 mmHg. Abdominal examination revealed a large, severely tender palpable mass in the right upper quadrant.
objective.routine_investigations: AST 516 U/L, ALT 722 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 1,930 U/L, total bilirubin 5.3 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 3.9 mg/dL, total protein 7.7 g/dL, albumin 3.8 g/dL, WBC 8,000/mm^3, hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL, platelets 426,000/mm^3, CRP 6 mg/dL, and ESR 40 mm/h. Coagulation profile: PT 13 sec, PTT 34 sec, INR 1. Serum amylase, blood glucose, sodium, potassium, BUN, and creatinine were normal. Venous blood gas: pH 7.5, HCO3 30 mmol/L, PCO2 37.9 mmHg. Viral hepatitis serology was positive for hepatitis A virus (HAV) IgM and negative for other viral hepatitis markers. Blood and urine cultures and serological titers for typhoid fever and brucellosis were all negative. Abdominal ultrasonography showed normal liver size and echogenicity with massive acalculous gallbladder distension (gallbladder hydrops measuring 130 x 50 mm, extending inferiorly near the iliac crest) with normal wall thickness and no stones.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Acute hepatitis A virus (HAV) infection complicated by acalculous gallbladder hydrops, confirmed by positive serum HAV IgM serology and abdominal ultrasonography. Typhoid fever, brucellosis, and bacterial sepsis were ruled out by negative serologies and sterile blood/urine cultures. Empiric intravenous ceftizoxime and metronidazole were administered initially for fever and toxic appearance and discontinued on hospital day 3 once fever resolved and blood cultures returned negative. With conservative medical management (no surgical intervention required), his abdominal pain and jaundice resolved by day 5, and he was discharged with close outpatient follow-up.
